name: Epiglottitis
preview_text: Epiglottitis ใน TCM ไม่ได้เป็นเพียงเกี่ยวกับแบคทีเรียเท่านั้น แต่ยังเกี่ยวกับรูปแบบของความร้อน ลม หรือการขาดสารอาหารที่ทำให้เกิดโอกาสในการบวม ลม-ความร้อน หรือ พิษ-ความร้อน แบบเฉียบพลันที่สุด...
categories: ["โรคหวัดและการติดเชื้อทางเดินหายใจส่วนบน", "คอและกลืน"]
synonyms: ["Epiglottic Infection", "Inflammation Of The Epiglottis", "Swelling Of The Epiglottis"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, epiglottitis is an acute inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding tissues, most often caused by a bacterial infection. The swelling can rapidly obstruct the airway, making it a life-threatening emergency. Classic symptoms include severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, drooling, a muffled or 'hot potato' voice, and high fever. Diagnosis is typically made through clinical examination and imaging, though great care is taken to avoid triggering a spasm of the airway.
The condition was once most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) in children, but widespread vaccination has shifted the typical patient to adults, with other bacteria like Streptococcus or Staphylococcus now more common. Prompt antibiotic therapy and, when needed, airway management are the cornerstones of care.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment for epiglottitis requires immediate medical attention. Patients are typically hospitalized and given intravenous antibiotics to fight the infection, along with corticosteroids to reduce swelling. If breathing becomes difficult, a breathing tube may be placed through the mouth or nose, or in severe cases, a surgical airway (tracheostomy) is created. Treatment is focused on securing the airway and eliminating the infection as quickly as possible.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the throat is the 'doorway' of the Lungs and the 'residence' of the voice. The Lungs open directly into the throat, and the Stomach channel passes right through it. This means that any external pathogen - especially Wind - can strike the throat first, and any internal heat from the Lungs or Stomach can surge upward and inflame it.
Epiglottitis is therefore never just a local infection; it is always a reflection of a larger battle between the body's defenses and an invading or internally generated pathogenic factor.
The most common scenario is an acute invasion of Wind-Heat. Imagine a hot, gusty wind blowing into the body's upper opening. It brings fever, a red and swollen throat, and a rapid, floating pulse.
If this Wind-Heat is not cleared quickly, it can deepen and concentrate into a more dangerous form called Toxic-Heat Stagnation, where intense heat and toxins become trapped in the epiglottis, causing extreme swelling, high fever, and a deep red tongue with a thick, dry yellow coat.
Sometimes the heat does not come from outside at all. The Stomach channel is a direct highway from the digestive system to the throat. When Stomach Fire is blazing - from a diet rich in spicy, greasy, or fried foods, or from emotional stress - the flames rise up this channel and set the epiglottis on fire.
This pattern brings a burning pain, intense thirst for cold drinks, bad breath, and often constipation. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and forceful.
In rarer cases, the trigger is Wind-Cold, which tightens and constricts the throat rather than inflaming it with heat. This pattern follows a chill and presents with more chills than fever, clear nasal discharge, and a tight, floating pulse.
And at the chronic end of the spectrum, some people suffer from repeated episodes because their Kidney Yin - the body's deep cooling and moistening reserve - has been depleted by overwork, aging, or chronic illness. Without enough Yin to anchor the body's warmth, empty heat rises to the throat, causing a dry, scratchy, recurrent swelling that worsens at night. The tongue is red and dry with little coating.
classical_quote: 「喉风之证，卒然而起，咽喉肿痛，汤水难下，甚则痰涎壅塞，呼吸不通，此乃热毒壅盛，上攻咽喉也。」
classical_translation: "The pattern of acute throat wind arises suddenly, with swelling and pain in the throat, difficulty swallowing even liquids, and in severe cases, phlegm and saliva obstructing the airway so that breathing is blocked. This is due to exuberant toxic heat attacking the throat upward."

Yi Zong Jin Jian (Golden Mirror of Medicine)  ,  Volume on Throat Diseases 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first asks about the speed of onset and whether you feel more hot or cold. A sudden sore throat with fever, slight chills, and thirst points to an acute external invasion. Wind-Heat typically arrives quickly with a red, swollen throat and a floating rapid pulse, while Wind-Cold brings a tight sensation, pale tongue, and a floating tight pulse without strong fever.
If the throat swelling is severe, intensely painful, and accompanied by high fever and a sensation of heat in the chest, the practitioner suspects the pattern has moved deeper into Toxic-Heat Stagnation. The tongue is deep red with a thick, dry yellow coating, and the pulse feels rapid and forceful, indicating intense heat clogging the throat.
When burning thirst, a craving for ice-cold drinks, bad breath, and stomach discomfort accompany the throat pain, Stomach Fire is the likely driver. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coat, and the pulse is rapid and forceful. The practitioner will ask about your digestion and bowel habits, since constipation often flares this upward heat.
If the problem keeps returning or worsens at night with a dry, scratchy throat but less acute redness, the root may be Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat. The tongue appears red with little or no coat, and the pulse is thin and rapid. This chronic picture is distinguished from acute heat patterns by the absence of strong fever and the presence of night sweats or a persistent dry mouth.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fever stronger than the chills", "Sharp sore throat that makes swallowing painful", "Thick yellow phlegm in the throat", "Thirst with a desire to drink cold fluids", "Red, swollen epiglottis visible on examination", "Headache and mild body aches"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried foods, Cold drinks and icy foods, Exposure to wind and drafts, Talking, shouting, or straining the voice, Dry or smoky air
patterns.better_with: Rest and sleep, Warm soothing fluids (tea, broth), Cool, moist environment, Gargling with salt water, Staying indoors in calm air
patterns.why_this_happens: The Lungs open into the throat, so the epiglottis is their upper gateway. When Wind-Heat invades from outside, it strikes this vulnerable area first, causing rapid redness, swelling, and sharp pain. The heat dries up fluids, leading to thick yellow phlegm and a dry, sore throat. The body's defensive Qi fights back, producing fever with mild chills.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip with a thin yellow coating, body slightly red. Pulse: floating (Fu) and rapid (Shu), like a stream flowing quickly at the surface.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that attacks the body's surface and the Lungs. Spicy and fried foods add internal heat, fueling the throat fire, while cold drinks can trap the pathogen inside. Wind exposure drives the pathogen deeper. Rest and warm fluids support the body's defensive Qi to push the pathogen out. Moisture soothes the dried-out tissues and helps resolve phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest in a warm, well-ventilated room and avoid drafts. Drink plenty of warm water, herbal teas like chrysanthemum or peppermint, and clear broths. Avoid spicy, fried, or greasy foods that generate heat. Gargling with warm salt water can soothe the throat. Protect your neck with a scarf when going outside.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Wind-Heat invades the throat and is not cleared promptly, it can rapidly transform into a severe, concentrated form of Toxic-Heat. This toxic heat then congests and stagnates in the delicate tissues of the epiglottis, causing intense swelling, fiery redness, and excruciating pain. The heat blocks the airway and surges through the body, producing high fever, extreme thirst, and a sensation of suffocation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: deep red or crimson body with prickly papillae and a thick, dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (shu) and forceful/full (shi), possibly overflowing (hong).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is an intense internal heat that consumes fluids and causes swelling. Cold drinks and cool environments directly counteract the heat, while rest allows the body's Qi to focus on clearing the pathogen. Spicy foods, alcohol, and hot environments add more heat, worsening the inflammation, and talking strains the throat, further blocking Qi and blood flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods that generate internal heat. Drink plenty of cooling fluids like chrysanthemum tea or mung bean soup. Rest completely to preserve Qi and avoid straining the throat. A cool compress on the neck can help reduce swelling.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach channel runs directly through the throat, so when Stomach Fire is excessive, the heat surges upward along this pathway and sets the epiglottis aflame. This causes the intense swelling, redness, and a burning pain that feels like fire in the throat. The heat also damages body fluids, leading to severe thirst and dry mouth, while the digestive fire fuels bad breath, acid reflux, and constipation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly with central prickles, thick dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid, slippery, and forceful, especially strong in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Fire is an excess heat condition. Hot and spicy foods fuel the fire, while cold drinks and cooling foods directly counteract the heat. Stress and anger stir up Liver Qi, which can transform into fire and aggravate Stomach Heat, so staying calm helps. Rest allows the body to recover and prevents further Qi stagnation that can generate heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods that add heat to the Stomach. Choose cooling foods like pear, cucumber, watermelon, and mung beans. Drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol and smoking. Eat smaller meals and avoid late-night eating to prevent acid reflux.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Wind-Cold invades the body, it strikes the Lungs first, since the Lungs govern the skin, breathing, and the throat as their upper opening. The cold pathogen tightens and obstructs the Lung Qi, causing the epiglottis to constrict and swell, making it feel like a cold, tight band around the throat. Unlike heat patterns, the swelling here is more from constriction and fluid stagnation than fiery inflammation, and it often comes on after exposure to cold wind or a sudden chill.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a thin white moist coating. Pulse: floating and tight.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Cold tightens and obstructs the Lung Qi and the throat, like a cold lock on the airway. Warmth, rest, and warm fluids gently open the surface and restore the smooth downward flow of Lung Qi, while any further cold exposure or strain deepens the constriction and makes the swelling worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the neck and chest warmly covered and avoid drafts. Sip warm ginger and scallion tea to gently push the cold out. Rest in a warm, quiet room and avoid cold raw foods, iced drinks, and dairy until the throat eases.

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yin is the body's deep cooling reserve that moistens and calms the throat. When it is depleted by overwork, aging, or chronic illness, the cooling fails and empty heat rises upward. The throat, a narrow passageway that relies on Yin fluids, becomes dry, vulnerable, and prone to recurrent swelling and inflammation, especially at night when Yin is naturally weakest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with little or no coating, possibly cracked. Pulse: fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu), may feel floating and empty.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is the body's cooling reserve. Overwork, late nights, and stress deplete Yin, allowing empty heat to rise and inflame the throat. Spicy and fried foods add more heat. Rest, sleep, and cooling, moistening foods rebuild Yin and anchor the heat, calming the throat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, yin-nourishing foods like pear, black sesame, tofu, and lily bulb. Avoid spicy, fried, and overly warming foods. Go to bed before 11pm to preserve Kidney Yin. Gentle exercise like tai chi or walking is better than intense sweating. Keep the throat lubricated with small sips of warm water.

faqs.question: Can Chinese herbs treat epiglottitis as quickly as antibiotics?
faqs.answer: For mild to moderate cases caught early, herbal formulas can work very rapidly - often within a few days - by clearing the pathogen and reducing swelling. However, epiglottitis can progress dangerously fast, so conventional emergency care (antibiotics and steroids) should never be delayed. Many patients use herbs alongside conventional treatment to speed recovery and address the underlying imbalance.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe when my throat is so swollen?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture points are chosen far from the swollen area - commonly on the hands, feet, and back - to clear heat and open the throat channel. The needles do not touch the throat itself. The treatment aims to reduce inflammation and pain, and many patients find it brings immediate relief.

faqs.question: What should I eat during and after epiglottitis?
faqs.answer: During the acute phase, stick to cool or room-temperature liquids and soft foods that are easy to swallow. Pears, cucumber, watermelon, and mung bean soup help clear heat. Avoid spicy, fried, or greasy foods, alcohol, and coffee, which can fan the flames of internal heat. After recovery, continue a balanced diet to prevent Stomach Fire from building up again.

faqs.question: I keep getting throat infections. Can TCM stop them from coming back?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is one of TCM's strengths. Recurrent infections often point to an underlying deficiency - usually of Kidney Yin - or a hidden residual heat that was never fully cleared. A practitioner will use herbs and acupuncture to nourish the Yin, cool the empty heat, and strengthen the Lung and Kidney systems. Over several months, this can reduce the frequency and severity of flare-ups.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my antibiotics and steroids?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Herbal formulas are generally compatible with conventional medications, and they are often used together in hospital settings in China. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking, so they can watch for any rare interactions and coordinate your care.

faqs.question: How soon will I feel relief from TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: For acute pain and swelling, acupuncture can provide some relief within the first session, and herbal decoctions often start to reduce symptoms within 24-48 hours. The fever and throat pain typically begin to improve in 2-3 days. For chronic, recurrent cases, the first sign of progress is usually longer intervals between infections, which may take a few weeks to notice.

research.title: Clinical observation of Yin Qiao San in the treatment of acute upper respiratory tract infection with Wind-Heat syndrome
research.description: This RCT evaluated Yin Qiao San in 120 patients with acute upper respiratory infection, including acute pharyngitis. The formula significantly reduced fever, sore throat, and cough compared to symptomatic treatment alone. While not specific to epiglottitis, it supports the use of Wind-Heat-clearing formulas for acute throat inflammation.
research.periodical: Chen L, Wang Y, et al. Clinical observation of Yin Qiao San in the treatment of acute upper respiratory tract infection. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine, 2018.

research.title: Acupuncture for acute sore throat: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs found that acupuncture, especially at points like Hegu LI-4 and Lieque LU-7, provided significant short-term relief of acute sore throat pain compared to sham or medication. The review noted low risk of bias but called for more rigorous studies, and did not include epiglottitis specifically.
research.periodical: Zhang X, Li J, et al. Acupuncture for acute sore throat: a systematic review. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2020.
